outline: Meaning, types and importance of production

modules.title: Production and the Factors of Production
modules.html:
1.1 Meaning of production

Production is any human activity that creates or adds utility (value) to goods and services in order to satisfy human wants. It is not complete until the commodity reaches the final consumer, so transport, storage, advertising and retailing are all productive.

1.2 Types of production

  1. Primary (extractive) — farming, mining, fishing, lumbering.
  2. Secondary (manufacturing and construction) — converting raw materials into finished goods.
  3. Tertiary (services) — direct services (teaching, medicine) and commercial services (trade, banking, insurance, transport).

1.3 The factors of production

FactorMeaningRewardKey features
LandAll free gifts of nature: soil, minerals, water, forestsRentFixed in supply, immobile geographically, subject to diminishing returns, no cost of production
LabourHuman effort, mental or physical, directed at productionWages/salariesCannot be separated from the worker, perishable, mobile but with resistance
CapitalMan-made wealth used to produce further wealthInterestDerived from saving; depreciates; can be fixed, working or social capital
EntrepreneurOrganiser who hires and combines other factors and bears riskProfitResidual, uncertain reward; may be negative (loss)

1.4 Efficiency and productivity

Productivity is output per unit of input:

$$ \text{Labour productivity} = \frac{\text{Total output}}{\text{Number of workers}} $$

It is raised by education and training, better capital equipment, improved management, incentives and good health.

1.5 Law of variable proportions

When one factor is varied while others are fixed, total product first rises at an increasing rate (increasing returns), then at a decreasing rate (diminishing returns), and may eventually fall (negative returns). This is the basis of the short-run cost curves studied in SSS 2.

examples.q: A farm employing 8 workers harvests 240 bags of maize; with 10 workers it harvests 280 bags. Compute average and marginal productivity.
examples.a: Average product with 8 workers = 240/8 = 30 bags; with 10 workers = 280/10 = 28 bags. Marginal product of the 2 extra workers = (280 − 240)/2 = 20 bags each. Average product has fallen, so the farm has entered the stage of diminishing returns.

examples.q: Why is land said to have no cost of production?
examples.a: Land is a free gift of nature; society did not incur any cost to create it. Costs such as clearing, draining or fencing are improvements to land, not the cost of producing land itself.

modules.title: Division of Labour, Scale of Production and Business Organisation
modules.html:
2.1 Division of labour and specialisation

Division of labour is the splitting of a production process into separate tasks, each performed by a different worker. Specialisation is the concentration of a worker, firm, region or country on the activity in which it is most efficient. Adam Smith illustrated it with the pin factory.

Advantages: higher output and productivity, saving of time, development of skill, use of machinery, lower unit cost, easier training.
Disadvantages: monotony and boredom, loss of craftsmanship, risk of unemployment when one process is mechanised, interdependence (a strike in one section halts all), decline of pride in work.

Limitations: size of the market, nature of the product, level of technology, availability of capital and of skilled labour.

2.2 Scale of production

The scale of production is the size of a firm's productive capacity. Expanding it may bring economies of scale (falling average cost) or, beyond the optimum, diseconomies of scale (rising average cost).

  • Internal economies — technical, managerial, marketing, financial, risk-bearing and research economies enjoyed by the individual firm as it grows.
  • External economies — benefits from the growth of the whole industry: skilled labour pool, specialist suppliers, shared infrastructure, trade journals.
  • Internal diseconomies — managerial overload, poor communication, bureaucracy, low morale.
  • External diseconomies — congestion, rising rents and wages, pollution as an area becomes overcrowded.

2.3 Business units

TypeOwnershipLiabilityCapital sources
Sole proprietorshipOne ownerUnlimitedPersonal savings, loans, trade credit
Partnership2–20 partners (deed of partnership)Unlimited except limited partnersPartners' contributions, loans
Private limited company (Ltd)2–50 shareholdersLimitedPrivate share issue, loans, debentures
Public limited company (PLC)7 to no maximumLimitedPublic share issue, debentures, retained profit
Cooperative societyMembers, one member one voteLimitedMembers' shares, dues, loans
Public corporationGovernmentState-backedGovernment subvention, loans, revenue

Companies are separate legal persons with perpetual succession, formed by filing a memorandum and articles of association; a PLC must issue a prospectus before selling shares to the public.

2.4 Location and localisation of industry

Factors determining location: nearness to raw materials, to markets, to power and water, transport, labour supply, land availability, government policy and historical accident. Localisation is the concentration of an industry in one area; delocalisation is the deliberate dispersal of industries to reduce congestion and spread development.

examples.q: State two reasons why a sole proprietorship may fail to grow large.
examples.a: (i) Limited capital — finance is restricted to the owner's savings and small loans, since shares cannot be sold to the public. (ii) Unlimited liability and limited managerial capacity — the owner bears all risk personally and cannot supervise a very large organisation, which discourages expansion.

examples.q: Distinguish between internal and external economies of scale.
examples.a: Internal economies arise from the growth of the individual firm itself (e.g. bulk buying, specialist managers, cheaper loans) and are within its control. External economies arise from the growth of the entire industry or locality (e.g. availability of trained labour, specialist ancillary firms, better roads) and benefit all firms in the industry regardless of their own size.

quiz.q: Production is said to be complete when:
options: Goods and services reach the final consumer
Goods are stored in a warehouse
quiz.solution: Utility is only fully created when the commodity is in the hands of the final consumer, so distribution and retailing are part of production.
The entrepreneur organises production and bears risk; the residual reward is profit, which may also be a loss.

quiz.q: Which factor of production is fixed in supply and geographically immobile?
quiz.solution: Land is a gift of nature, its total quantity cannot be increased and it cannot be moved from one place to another.

quiz.q: Mining and fishing belong to which type of production?
quiz.solution: Primary or extractive production takes resources directly from nature.

quiz.q: A major disadvantage of division of labour is:
quiz.solution: Repeating one narrow task makes work monotonous and can reduce job satisfaction and craftsmanship.

quiz.q: Division of labour is chiefly limited by:
quiz.solution: Splitting work into many tasks is only profitable if output can be sold in large quantities, so market size is the main limit.

options: Output divided by number of workers
quiz.solution: Labour productivity is output per worker, that is total output divided by the number of workers employed.

quiz.q: Capital differs from land because capital is:
quiz.solution: Capital is man-made wealth used to produce further wealth and is created out of saving.

quiz.q: In a private limited company, the maximum number of shareholders is:
quiz.solution: A private limited company may have between 2 and 50 members and cannot invite the general public to buy its shares.

quiz.q: Which business unit has unlimited liability?
quiz.solution: A sole proprietor is not a separate legal person, so personal assets can be seized to settle business debts.

quiz.q: A document inviting the public to buy shares in a company is a:
quiz.solution: A prospectus is the statutory invitation to the public to subscribe for shares or debentures.

quiz.q: Perpetual succession means that a company:
options: Continues to exist despite the death of members
quiz.solution: As a separate legal person, the company's life is independent of the lives of its shareholders.

quiz.q: Diseconomies of scale cause average cost to:
quiz.solution: Beyond the optimum size, managerial and communication problems push average cost upward.

quiz.q: The concentration of an industry in a particular area is called:
quiz.solution: Localisation is the geographical concentration of an industry, often because of raw materials, power or historic advantage.

quiz.q: Which of these is an internal economy of scale?
options: Availability of skilled labour in the area
Bulk buying discounts to a large firm
Growth of specialist suppliers in the industry
quiz.solution: Bulk buying discounts arise from the firm's own expansion, hence internal; the others come from growth of the industry or locality.

quiz.q: In a cooperative society, voting is based on:
quiz.solution: Cooperatives are democratic bodies: each member has a single vote irrespective of shareholding.

quiz.q: The law of variable proportions applies when:
options: One factor is varied while others are fixed
quiz.solution: It describes short-run behaviour of output when a variable factor is added to fixed factors, producing increasing then diminishing returns.
